title: Modification of a Quantum-inspired Genetic Algorithm for Numerical Optimization Using Qudit under Conditions of Simulating Quantum Decoherence
abstract_summary: The paper proposes a modified quantum-inspired genetic algorithm (MQIGA) that models classical GA operations via qudits and simulates quantum decoherence by using a density-matrix Bloch-sphere analogue based on Heisenberg–Weyl operators and injecting Gaussian noise into quantum gates. Detailed pseudocode is provided and the method is evaluated on benchmark optimization functions, a hybrid flow-shop cost scheduling problem, and extreme learning machine tuning, demonstrating improved solution accuracy, faster convergence to global maxima, and competitive runtime versus standard QIGA and several classical metaheuristics.
methodology_description: The paper develops a modified quantum-inspired genetic algorithm (MQIGA) for numerical optimization that models qudit-based quantum operations and simulates quantum decoherence. States of multilevel quantum genes (qudits) are represented via a density matrix expansion in the Heisenberg–Weyl operator basis (an analogue of the Bloch-sphere for d-level systems). Initialization applies a generalized Hadamard transform for qudits to generate uniform superposition amplitudes; these amplitudes are combined with the density matrix to obtain per-level probability amplitudes. Decoherence / environmental noise is simulated by perturbing rotation angles with a normal random variable ξ ~ N(0,1) scaled by an error level τ (θ = τ ξ). Genetic operators are implemented as follows: measurement produces classical binary chromosomes from qudit probabilities; crossover is realized by applying rotation gates on the qudit Bloch-like representation with shifted angles Δ based on comparisons to the best chromosome; mutation is effected by probabilistically reversing qudit state vectors according to population-level mutation frequency and per-gene mutation probability. The algorithm is specified in detailed pseudocode (Algs. 1–8) and iterates initialization → measurement → fitness evaluation → quantum-gate based update (rotations with simulated noise) → crossover → mutation until stopping criteria. MQIGA is compared experimentally to QIGA (baseline quantum-inspired GA) and classical metaheuristics (GA, DE, PSO, NRO, ACOR) on (a) standard benchmark optimization functions (Rastrigin, Sphere, Griewank, Schwefel 1.2, Ackley, Rosenbrock, Zakharov, Styblinski–Tang) in 2 and 15 dimensions, (b) an applied hybrid flow-shop production-planning cost maximization problem (three hypothetical scenarios), and (c) as a global optimizer for tuning input weights/biases of Extreme Learning Machine (ELM) regressors on three public datasets. Experiments report best, mean, standard deviation over multiple runs, run time, convergence curves, and Wilcoxon statistical tests. Implementation used Python (JupyterLab) and the MEALPY metaheuristics library; all algorithm hyperparameters and experiment protocols (population size, chromosome length, qudit length, τ, mutation rates, number of iterations, number of repeats) are explicitly listed.
experimental_setup: Experiments executed in JupyterLab on a classical workstation with Intel Core i9-13980HX and 32 GB RAM. Quantum behavior is simulated numerically: qudit states represented via density matrices using Heisenberg–Weyl operators; noise/decoherence injected by sampling standard normal N(0,1) and scaling by τ to perturb rotation angles in quantum gates. No physical QPU or quantum simulator package name is reported.
dataset_used: Benchmark mathematical functions (Rastrigin, Sphere, Griewank, Schwefel 1.2, Ackley, Rosenbrock, Zakharov, Styblinski–Tang) with search ranges as given in the paper; production planning hypothetical control scenarios J10c5a2, J10c5b1, J10c5c1 (10 jobs, 5 stages, specified machine configurations); three public regression datasets used for ELM tuning: CPU Performance (10 features, 209 samples), Auto Imports (26 features, 206 samples), Boston Housing (14 features, 506 samples). No proprietary financial market time-series data were used.

pipeline_steps: Initialize MQIGA hyperparameters (pop_size, chrom_len, qudit_len, τ, mutation frequency, mutation probability, max generations).
For each qudit-state apply generalized Hadamard (Hd) to set initial superposition amplitudes.
Construct density matrix ρ using Heisenberg–Weyl operator basis and compute amplitude vectors = Hd|ψ〉 * ρ.
Convert complex amplitudes to existence probabilities Pr_n = |α_n|^2; sample/measure to obtain classical binary genes and decode to integer phenotype.
Evaluate fitness f(phenotype) for each chromosome (benchmarks, cost function, or MAE objective for ELM tuning).
Record best solution and statistics (best, mean, std).
Update quantum-population Q(t) using rotation gates U(θ) where θ include noise: θ = τ * N(0,1) (simulate decoherence).
Crossover: apply rotated updates with offset Δθ based on comparison with best chromosome; update qcv probabilities via density-matrix multiplication.
Mutation: with population-level frequency pop_mut and per-gene probability mut_prob, perform reversal of qudit-state vectors (index reordering) to produce n_qcv.
Measure to produce new classical population and repeat until gen_max.
Collect outputs: best values per run, averages over repeated runs, run time, and convergence curves; perform Wilcoxon tests vs baselines.

metrics_reported: mean of best values across runs (μ)
Wilcoxon nonparametric p-values comparing MQIGA vs baselines
For ELM tuning: Mean Absolute Error (MAE) via 10-fold cross-validation
experiment_output.output_format: Tabular results per function/experiment (b, μ, σ, t), convergence plots, Wilcoxon test tables, and ELM MAE tables

quantum_simulation_params.rotation_gate: U(θ) general 2D rotation and generalized Hd for qudits
quantum_simulation_params.noise_model: angle perturbation θ = τ * ξ where ξ ~ N(0,1)

reproducibility_notes: The paper provides detailed pseudocode for all algorithm components (Algs. 1–8), explicit hyperparameter settings, experiment protocols (population, iterations, repeats), and identifies use of MEALPY and Python/JupyterLab. Datasets used are public / standardized benchmark functions and named public datasets (CPU Performance, Auto Imports, Boston Housing). However, no code repository, implementation artifacts, or exact random seeds are provided in the paper, so full bitwise reproducibility is not ensured without author-supplied code. The algorithm can be reimplemented from the provided pseudocode and parameter tables, but small implementation choices (matrix arithmetic details, random number generator seeds, numerical tolerances) may affect exact outcomes.
key_findings: [supported] The proposed MQIGA (modified quantum-inspired genetic algorithm using qudits and simulated decoherence) outperformed the baseline QIGA and several classical metaheuristics (GA, DE, PSO, NRO) on the authors' benchmark optimization experiments in terms of solution accuracy, convergence speed and (in many cases) execution time.

[supported] On 2-dimensional benchmark functions (f1–f8) MQIGA reached the global maximum in 100% of runs reported and achieved equal or better best / mean / std-dev statistics compared with QIGA and most classical algorithms in the experiments.

[supported] On 15-dimensional benchmark functions MQIGA reached the global maximum in 75% of the experiments and was among the fastest methods for several test functions (specifically faster than QIGA and GA on f1–f3 in the authors' tests).

[supported] For the applied hybrid flow-shop production planning instances tested, MQIGA obtained the best or near-best objective values in the reported scenarios (examples: J10c5a2 best b = 1234.2600) while keeping runtime comparable to other heuristics.

[supported] When used to tune input weights and biases of compact Extreme Learning Machines (ELM), MQIGA-ELM produced substantially improved generalization MAE versus an untuned ELM and versus other optimizer-tuned ELM variants in the experiments (examples: CPU Performance MAE improved from 12.9 to 5.3; Boston Housing MAE improved from 3.35 to 1.86).

[supported] Nonparametric Wilcoxon tests reported in the paper indicate statistically significant superiority (p < 0.05) of MQIGA over many baseline algorithms on numerous benchmark functions (the paper reports many p-values < 0.05 in pairwise comparisons).

[speculative] The paper proposes modeling quantum decoherence in the quantum-inspired operators by injecting a normal random variable (N(0,1)) scaled by an error level τ into quantum gates as an emulator of NISQ-era noise; this modeling choice is proposed and used but is not validated against physical device noise beyond conceptual justification.

[speculative] The authors present a density-matrix / Heisenberg–Weyl-operator based representation as an analogue of the Bloch sphere for qudits and claim it enables state-rotation operations for multilevel systems within the MQIGA framework; this is presented as a methodological extension rather than a formal proof of superiority.

[supported] MQIGA performance depends on hyperparameter choices (population size, chromosome length, qudit length, noise/error level τ, mutation frequency/probability); the authors note and demonstrate sensitivity across experiments.

[speculative] The authors suggest possible future extensions (support for minimization, improved convergence robustness, automated hyperparameter tuning, multi-objective formulation) — these are proposed directions rather than demonstrated results.
results_summary: The paper introduces MQIGA, a quantum-inspired genetic optimizer that represents genes using qudits and simulates NISQ-like decoherence by injecting Gaussian noise into quantum-gate-like operations. Across a battery of experiments (2D and 15D benchmark functions, three hybrid flow-shop planning instances, and ELM hyperparameter tuning), MQIGA achieved better or comparable best/mean/std-dev results versus a baseline QIGA and several classical metaheuristics, often converging faster and with competitive runtime. Statistical tests (Wilcoxon) reported significant improvements on many functions. MQIGA-ELM notably reduced MAE on regression datasets compared with an untuned ELM and other optimizer-tuned ELMs. The authors present the qudit-density-matrix formalism (Heisenberg–Weyl basis) as a Bloch-sphere analogue and recommend further work on robustness, hyperparameter automation and multi-objective extensions.

quantum_advantage_detail: The work is 'quantum-inspired' and implemented classically (no quantum hardware or provable quantum complexity advantage). The paper demonstrates empirical heuristic improvements in selected benchmarking and application scenarios, but does not claim nor prove a formal quantum computational advantage (e.g., asymptotic speedup or quantum supremacy). The use of qudit-inspired representations and simulated decoherence is a methodological, not a hardware-backed, approach, so any implication of 'quantum advantage' remains speculative and empirical rather than theoretically demonstrated.

MQIGA не даёт универсального превосходства: в ряде случаев (особенно на некоторых многомерных функциях: f3, f8 при n=15 и др.) алгоритм демонстрирует худшие результаты по сравнению с некоторыми альтернативами (авторское заявление / экспериментальное наблюдение).
Результаты зависят от выбранного уровня ошибки τ (моделирования шума) и других выборок параметров — требуется настройка для каждой задачи (авторское заявление).
